question: During the harvest season, wild animals are often seriously injured by combine harvesters, especially by the cutting unit1. The resulting mutilation can lead to an agonising death2. This is not only a problem of species protection or animal welfare, but also requires action from a health-policy perspective, as it can result in contamination of the crop. These risks to food and feed production must be minimised, which can be ensured by using thermal drones. 1.
What long-term strategy does the Commission envisage to protect wild animals during the harvest season and thus also ensure consumer protection?

What concrete measures does the Commission plan to undertake to raise awareness across the EU of the problem of wild animal mutilation3, to promote mesures to prevent it, to reduce regulatory barriers for technical solutions and to provide funding?
Does the Commission plan to recommend or mandate that Member States establish thermal drone programmes to protect wild animals?

Roe deer fawns have no flight reflex, their only form of protection is to crouch down motionless. In Germany alone, around 90 000 fawns die in this way every year. This particularly concerns fawns, but other wild animals are also affected.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.11.2024) It is for the national and regional authorities in the Member States, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders, to identify and implement the most appropriate measures to prevent damage to protected species under the Birds1 and Habitats2 Directives during agricultural harvest operations.

The use of thermal drones, as suggested by the Honourable Members, could be one of the solutions available. Under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)3, Member States can also support measures to prevent damage to wildlife during agricultural harvest operations, provided this is in line with their CAP Strategic plan4.

In line with EU nature legislation, the Commission supports using drones and other technologies where they can contribute to the recovery of species threatened by mowing - or harvesting - induced mortality, such as Little bustard, Montagu’s harrier and Corncrake.

These technologies, including thermal drones, might also be beneficial in assisting with rescuing common wildlife and game species not protected under EU nature legislation. The EU Animal Health Law5 does not provide for any specific measures to address the impact of wildlife on crops.

From a food and feed safety perspective, there are no specific measures provided either, but general hygiene requirements laid down in Union legislation apply when placing food and feed on the market. The Commission is not aware of EU regulatory obstacles to a more widespread use of thermal drones to protect wildlife from being accidentally killed by agricultural activities.

Where drones need be operated close to more risky areas such as densely populated areas or airports, or with a longer range, operators need to pay additional care as required by the Regulation (EU) 2019/9476.
1 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the

conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25. 2 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 3 https://agriculture.ec.europa.eu/common-agricultural-policy_en 4 https://agriculture.ec.europa.

eu/cap-my-country/cap-strategic-plans_en 5 Regulation (EU) 2016/429 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 9 March 2016 on transmissible animal diseases and amending and repealing certain acts in the area of animal health (‘Animal Health Law’), OJ L 84, 31.3.2016, p. 1–208.
6 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/947 of 24 May 2019 on the rules and procedures for the operation of unmanned aircraft, OJ L 152, 11.6.2019, p. 45–71.
